Overview

About the atlas

The atlas brings together reports of border closures and restrictions between 21 October 2016 and 21 October 2026. It documents past events and the evidence behind them; it does not provide live information about whether a border is open.

What is a record? A record is an entry compiled for this dataset from one or more sources. It describes a restriction affecting a specified crossing, group of crossings or wider border policy. It may contain several dated phases as the restriction changes.

What does the dataset cover?

The main dataset describes restrictions at land borders and international river ferries, including restrictions on particular travellers or goods. Related entries can describe different parts of the same event, so the number of records is not a count of independent closure decisions.

Routine overnight opening hours, individual visa refusals and checks that allow passage are excluded. The main dataset does not cover airports or sea-only restrictions; the selected island-state policies shown on the map are explained separately below.

How should I read the map?

The reason given for a restriction is indicated by its colour; the Map key explains the colours and symbols. Small dots mark named crossings. Their size does not show duration, severity or the number of records.

Lines represent broader restrictions, such as a border-wide rule or a rule affecting several crossings whose precise extent is not established. A solid line means the source explicitly describes a border-wide rule; a dotted line means its geographical extent is limited or uncertain. The line does not, by itself, establish that every crossing along it was closed. Locations are matched to each dated phase, so an entry can change from a line to a point as its scope changes.

Some named crossings have not yet been located with enough confidence to place a dot on the map. Their entries remain available in search and downloads and are included in the relevant counts. Crossing positions that are shown may be approximate. Read each entry for the affected people, goods, routes and exceptions. Unmarked does not necessarily mean open.

Read the location review and sources ↗

What do the dates mean?

Observed closure means a source reports that passage was stopped or restricted. Policy in force gives the dates of a rule. Announced closure dates come from a planned schedule. Repeated closures describes a period with closures and possible openings.

A record can appear in a month without covering every day of it. When the evidence gives only individual dates, or dates are disputed, the map shows those dates without filling the gaps. A last report of closure is not treated as a reopening date. Missing end dates are not extended to the present.

Days are calculated from recorded calendar dates. Same-day closures have no whole-day total; overlapping periods should not be added together.

How are the reasons grouped?

The categories, labelled “coded rationale” in the records, summarise reasons given in the sources. More than one category can apply to a record. An official explanation is recorded as such; it may not explain every reason for a closure.

Grey means no category has been assigned. This can reflect missing evidence or a reason that does not fit the categories.

Coverage varies by place, time and available sources. The charts describe the records collected. They do not measure how often closures happen worldwide. The duration charts use only land-border records with sufficiently clear dates and reopening evidence.

How do I find and download records?

Use Search & zoom to choose a continent or search across all recorded dates. Click a coloured border, crossing dot or list entry to read its summary, dates and source links. Read all records opens a wider reading view.

Click the date above the timeline to choose a month and year directly. Play timeline moves through the months; the speed control offers 1×, 2×, 4× and 8× playback.

The Dataset tab provides a searchable browser view and the complete Excel workbook. Download CSV saves matching entries as a spreadsheet. Save view saves an image of the map and its key.

How can I check the sources?

Each record links to its sources and explains any uncertainty. A later review may establish a more precise date, clarify who or what was affected, revise the reason assigned to a restriction, or show that an earlier claim is unsupported. The current entry reflects the latest assessment; earlier findings remain in the review history so the changes can be traced.

Some sources were available in full; others only as extracts. Different websites can repeat the same original report, so the number of links is not a count of independent confirmations.

Island borders during COVID-19

Selected pandemic border rules for Australia, New Zealand and the UK appear separately on the map as outlines. Leaving these cases unmarked would misleadingly suggest that their borders were accessible during the pandemic. Each record explains who was affected and the exceptions. These additions are excluded from the land-border analysis.
